Phosphorus

The name [[i:phosphorus]] comes from the Greek words meaning [[i:light bringing.]] When phosphorus was first isolated, scientists noted that it glowed in the dark and burned when exposed to air. Phosphorus is the only member of its group that does not occur in the uncombined state in nature; it exists in many allotropic forms. We will consider two of those forms: white phosphorus and red phosphorus.

White phosphorus is a white, waxy solid that melts at 44.2 °C and boils at 280 °C. It is insoluble in water (in which it is stored—see [[xref:CNX_Chem_18_04_Phosphorus]]), is very soluble in carbon disulfide, and bursts into flame in air. As a solid, as a liquid, as a gas, and in solution, white phosphorus exists as P[[sub:4]] molecules with four phosphorus atoms at the corners of a regular tetrahedron, as illustrated in [[xref:CNX_Chem_18_04_Phosphorus]]. Each phosphorus atom covalently bonds to the other three atoms in the molecule by single covalent bonds. White phosphorus is the most reactive allotrope and is very toxic.

(a) Because white phosphorus bursts into flame in air, it is stored in water. (b) The structure of white phosphorus consists of P[[sub:4]] molecules arranged in a tetrahedron. (c) Red phosphorus is much less reactive than is white phosphorus. (d) The structure of red phosphorus consists of networks of P[[sub:4]] tetrahedra joined by P-P single bonds. (credit a: modification of work from http://images-of-elements.com/phosphorus.php)

Two photos and two diagrams are shown and labeled “a,” “b,” “c,” and “d.” Photo a shows a test tube that contains a solid yellow compound. Diagram b shows a four-sided pyramid shape that has an atom at each corner. Photo c shows a dark black powder in a watch glass. Diagram d shows two four-sided pyramid shapes that have an atom at each corner and are connected together by a single bond.

Heating white phosphorus to 270–300 °C in the absence of air yields red phosphorus. Red phosphorus (shown in [[xref:CNX_Chem_18_04_Phosphorus]]) is denser, has a higher melting point (~600 °C), is much less reactive, is essentially nontoxic, and is easier and safer to handle than is white phosphorus. Its structure is highly polymeric and appears to contain three-dimensional networks of P[[sub:4]] tetrahedra joined by P-P single bonds. Red phosphorus is insoluble in solvents that dissolve white phosphorus. When red phosphorus is heated, P[[sub:4]] molecules sublime from the solid.

Sulfur

The allotropy of sulfur is far greater and more complex than that of any other element. Sulfur is the brimstone referred to in the Bible and other places, and references to sulfur occur throughout recorded history—right up to the relatively recent discovery that it is a component of the atmospheres of Venus and of Io, a moon of Jupiter. The most common and most stable allotrope of sulfur is yellow, rhombic sulfur, so named because of the shape of its crystals. Rhombic sulfur is the form to which all other allotropes revert at room temperature. Crystals of rhombic sulfur melt at 113 °C. Cooling this liquid gives long needles of monoclinic sulfur. This form is stable from 96 °C to the melting point, 119 °C. At room temperature, it gradually reverts to the rhombic form.

Both rhombic sulfur and monoclinic sulfur contain S[[sub:8]] molecules in which atoms form eight-membered, puckered rings that resemble crowns, as illustrated in [[xref:CNX_Chem_18_04_Sulfrchain]]. Each sulfur atom is bonded to each of its two neighbors in the ring by covalent S-S single bonds.

These four sulfur allotropes show eight-membered, puckered rings. Each sulfur atom bonds to each of its two neighbors in the ring by covalent S-S single bonds. Here are (a) individual S[[sub:8]] rings, (b) S[[sub:8]] chains formed when the rings open, (c) longer chains formed by adding sulfur atoms to S[[sub:8]] chains, and (d) part of the very long sulfur chains formed at higher temperatures.

Four diagrams are shown and labeled “a,” “b,” “c,” and “d.” Diagram a shows four ring structures that are each made up of eight single bonded atoms. Diagram b shows four chains of eight atoms. Diagram c shows three chains of atoms, one composed by nine atoms, one by twelve atoms and one by eleven atoms. Diagram d shows the same three chains, but this time they are much closer together and slightly intertwined.

When rhombic sulfur melts, the straw-colored liquid is quite mobile; its viscosity is low because S[[sub:8]] molecules are essentially spherical and offer relatively little resistance as they move past each other. As the temperature rises, S-S bonds in the rings break, and polymeric chains of sulfur atoms result. These chains combine end to end, forming still longer chains that tangle with one another. The liquid gradually darkens in color and becomes so viscous that finally (at about 230 °C) it does not pour easily. The dangling atoms at the ends of the chains of sulfur atoms are responsible for the dark red color because their electronic structure differs from those of sulfur atoms that have bonds to two adjacent sulfur atoms. This causes them to absorb light differently and results in a different visible color. Cooling the liquid rapidly produces a rubberlike amorphous mass, called plastic sulfur.

Sulfur boils at 445 °C and forms a vapor consisting of S[[sub:2]], S[[sub:6]], and S[[sub:8]] molecules; at about 1000 °C, the vapor density corresponds to the formula S[[sub:2]], which is a paramagnetic molecule like O[[sub:2]] with a similar electronic structure and a weak sulfur-sulfur double bond.

As seen in this discussion, an important feature of the structural behavior of the nonmetals is that the elements usually occur with eight electrons in their valence shells. If necessary, the elements form enough covalent bonds to supplement the electrons already present to possess an octet. For example, members of group 15 have five valence electrons and require only three additional electrons to fill their valence shells. These elements form three covalent bonds in their free state: triple bonds in the N[[sub:2]] molecule or single bonds to three different atoms in arsenic and phosphorus. The elements of group 16 require only two additional electrons. Oxygen forms a double bond in the O[[sub:2]] molecule, and sulfur, selenium, and tellurium form two single bonds in various rings and chains. The halogens form diatomic molecules in which each atom is involved in only one bond. This provides the electron required necessary to complete the octet on the halogen atom. The noble gases do not form covalent bonds to other noble gas atoms because they already have a filled outer shell.

Key Concepts and Summary

Nonmetals have structures that are very different from those of the metals, primarily because they have greater electronegativity and electrons that are more tightly bound to individual atoms. Most nonmetal oxides are acid anhydrides, meaning that they react with water to form acidic solutions. Molecular structures are common for most of the nonmetals, and several have multiple allotropes with varying physical properties.

Ástæðurnar fyrir þessu eru meðal annars minni stærð, meiri jónunarorka og (mikilvægast) sú staðreynd að fyrsti meðlimur hvers flokks hefur aðeins fjögur gildissvigrúm (eitt 2[[i:s]] og þrjú 2[[i:p]]) tiltæk fyrir tengi, á meðan aðrir meðlimir flokksins hafa tóm [[i:d]]-svigrúm í gildisskeljum sínum, sem gerir fimm, sex eða jafnvel fleiri tengi í kringum miðjuatómið möguleg. Til dæmis myndar köfnunarefni aðeins NF[[sub:3,]] en fosfór myndar bæði PF[[sub:3]] og PF[[sub:5]]."},{"key":"m68832:para:fs-idm105671392","en":"Another difference between the first group member and subsequent members is the greater ability of the first member to form [[i:π]] bonds. This is primarily a function of the smaller size of the first member of each group, which allows better overlap of atomic orbitals. Nonmetals, other than the first member of each group, rarely form π bonds to nonmetals that are the first member of a group. For example, sulfur-oxygen π bonds are well known, whereas sulfur does not normally form stable π bonds to itself.","is":"Annar munur á fyrsta meðlimi flokksins og síðari meðlimum er meiri hæfni fyrsta meðlimsins til að mynda [[i:π]]-tengi. Þetta er fyrst og fremst háð minni stærð fyrsta meðlimsins í hverjum flokki, sem leyfir betri skörun atómsvigrúma. Aðrir málmleysingjar en fyrsti meðlimur hvers flokks mynda sjaldan π-tengi við málmleysingja sem eru fyrsti meðlimur flokks. Til dæmis eru brennisteins-súrefnis π-tengi vel þekkt, en brennisteinn myndar venjulega ekki stöðug π-tengi við sjálfan sig."},{"key":"m68832:para:fs-idm175306688","en":"The variety of oxidation states displayed by most of the nonmetals means that many of their chemical reactions involve changes in oxidation state through oxidation-reduction reactions. There are five general aspects of the oxidation-reduction chemistry:","is":"Fjölbreytni oxunarástanda sem flestir málmleysingjar sýna þýðir að mörg efnahvörf þeirra fela í sér breytingar á oxunarástandi með oxunar-afoxunarhvörfum. Það eru fimm almennir þættir í oxunar-afoxunarefnafræðinni:"},{"key":"m68832:item:fs-idm145782848-item-1","en":"Nonmetals oxidize most metals. The oxidation state of the metal becomes positive as it undergoes oxidation and that of the nonmetal becomes negative as it undergoes reduction. For example:[[BR]] [[MATH:1]]","is":"Málmleysingjar oxa flesta málma. Oxunarástand málmsins verður jákvætt þegar hann oxast og oxunarástand málmleysingjans verður neikvætt þegar hann afoxast. Til dæmis:[[BR]] [[MATH:1]]"},{"key":"m68832:item:fs-idm145782848-item-2","en":"With the exception of nitrogen and carbon, which are poor oxidizing agents, a more electronegative nonmetal oxidizes a less electronegative nonmetal or the anion of the nonmetal:[[BR]] [[MATH:2]] [[MATH:3]]","is":"Að undanskildu köfnunarefni og kolefni, sem eru lélegir oxarar, oxar rafneikvæðari málmleysingi minna rafneikvæðan málmleysingja eða anjón málmleysingjans:[[BR]] [[MATH:2]] [[MATH:3]]"},{"key":"m68832:item:fs-idm145782848-item-3","en":"Fluorine and oxygen are the strongest oxidizing agents within their respective groups; each oxidizes all the elements that lie below it in the group. Within any period, the strongest oxidizing agent is in group 17. A nonmetal often oxidizes an element that lies to its left in the same period. For example:[[BR]] [[MATH:4]]","is":"Flúor og súrefni eru sterkustu oxararnir innan sinna flokka; hvor um sig oxar öll frumefnin sem liggja fyrir neðan það í flokknum. Innan hverrar lotu er sterkasti oxarinn í flokki 17. Málmleysingi oxar oft frumefni sem liggur vinstra megin við hann í sömu lotu. Til dæmis:[[BR]] [[MATH:4]]"},{"key":"m68832:item:fs-idm145782848-item-4","en":"The stronger a nonmetal is as an oxidizing agent, the more difficult it is to oxidize the anion formed by the nonmetal. This means that the most stable negative ions are formed by elements at the top of the group or in group 17 of the period.","is":"Því sterkari sem málmleysingi er sem oxari, því erfiðara er að oxa anjónina sem málmleysinginn myndar. Þetta þýðir að stöðugustu neikvæðu jónirnar eru myndaðar af frumefnum efst í flokknum eða í flokki 17 lotunnar."},{"key":"m68832:item:fs-idm145782848-item-5","en":"Fluorine and oxygen are the strongest oxidizing elements known. Fluorine does not form compounds in which it exhibits positive oxidation states; oxygen exhibits a positive oxidation state only when combined with fluorine. For example:[[BR]] [[MATH:5]]","is":"Flúor og súrefni eru sterkustu oxandi frumefnin sem þekkt eru. Flúor myndar ekki efnasambönd þar sem það hefur jákvætt oxunarástand; súrefni hefur aðeins jákvætt oxunarástand þegar það er í efnasambandi með flúor. Til dæmis:[[BR]] [[MATH:5]]"},{"key":"m68832:para:fs-idm159525136","en":"With the exception of most of the noble gases, all nonmetals form compounds with oxygen, yielding covalent oxides. Most of these oxides are acidic, that is, they react with water to form oxyacids. Recall from the acid-base chapter that an oxyacid is an acid consisting of hydrogen, oxygen, and some other element. Notable exceptions are carbon monoxide, CO, nitrous oxide, N[[sub:2]]O, and nitric oxide, NO. There are three characteristics of these acidic oxides:","is":"Að undanskildum flestum eðallofttegundum mynda allir málmleysingjar efnasambönd með súrefni og gefa af sér samgild oxíð. Flest þessara oxíða eru súr, það er að segja, þau hvarfast við vatn og mynda oxósýrur. Rifjum upp úr kaflanum um sýrur og basa að oxósýra er sýra sem samanstendur af vetni, súrefni og einhverju öðru frumefni. Helstu undantekningar eru kolmónoxíð, CO, hláturgas, N[[sub:2]]O, og nituroxíð, NO. Þessi súru oxíð hafa þrjú einkenni:"},{"key":"m68832:item:fs-idm120122192-item-1","en":"Oxides such as SO[[sub:2]] and N[[sub:2]]O[[sub:5]], in which the nonmetal exhibits one of its common oxidation states, are [[term:acid anhydrides|term-00001]] and react with water to form acids with no change in oxidation state. The product is an oxyacid. For example:[[BR]] [[MATH:6]] [[MATH:7]]","is":"Oxíð eins og SO[[sub:2]] og N[[sub:2]]O[[sub:5]], þar sem málmleysinginn hefur eitt af algengum oxunarástöndum sínum, eru [[term:sýruanhýdríð|term-00001]] og hvarfast við vatn til að mynda sýrur án breytinga á oxunarástandi. Myndefnið er oxósýra. Til dæmis:[[BR]] [[MATH:6]] [[MATH:7]]"},{"key":"m68832:item:fs-idm120122192-item-2","en":"Those oxides such as NO[[sub:2]] and ClO[[sub:2]], in which the nonmetal does not exhibit one of its common oxidation states, also react with water. In these reactions, the nonmetal is both oxidized and reduced. For example:[[BR]] [[MATH:8]][[BR]]Reactions in which the same element is both oxidized and reduced are called [[term:disproportionation reactions|term-00002]].","is":"Þau oxíð eins og NO[[sub:2]] og ClO[[sub:2]], þar sem málmleysinginn hefur ekki eitt af algengum oxunarástöndum sínum, hvarfast einnig við vatn. Í þessum efnahvörfum er málmleysinginn bæði oxaður og afoxaður. Til dæmis:[[BR]] [[MATH:8]][[BR]]Efnahvörf þar sem sama frumefnið er bæði oxað og afoxað kallast [[term:misvægishvörf|term-00002]]."},{"key":"m68832:item:fs-idm120122192-item-3","en":"The acid strength increases as the electronegativity of the central atom increases. To learn more, see the discussion in the chapter on acid-base chemistry.","is":"Sýrustyrkurinn eykst eftir því sem rafneikvæðni miðatónsins eykst. Til að læra meira, sjá umfjöllunina í kaflanum um efnafræði sýra og basa."},{"key":"m68832:para:fs-idm217428112","en":"The binary hydrogen compounds of the nonmetals also exhibit an acidic behavior in water, although only HCl, HBr, and HI are strong acids. The acid strength of the nonmetal hydrogen compounds increases from left to right across a period and down a group. For example, ammonia, NH[[sub:3]], is a weaker acid than is water, H[[sub:2]]O, which is weaker than is hydrogen fluoride, HF. Water, H[[sub:2]]O, is also a weaker acid than is hydrogen sulfide, H[[sub:2]]S[[sub:,]] which is weaker than is hydrogen selenide, H[[sub:2]]Se. Weaker acidic character implies greater basic character.","is":"Tvíundar vetnisefnasambönd málmleysingja sýna einnig súra hegðun í vatni, þó aðeins HCl, HBr og HI séu sterkar sýrur. Sýrustyrkur vetnisefnasambanda málmleysingja eykst frá vinstri til hægri yfir lotu og niður flokk. Til dæmis er ammoníak, NH[[sub:3]], veikari sýra en vatn, H[[sub:2]]O, sem er veikari en vetnisflúoríð, HF. Vatn, H[[sub:2]]O, er einnig veikari sýra en brennisteinsvetni, H[[sub:2]]S[[sub:,]] sem er veikari en vetnisselenið, H[[sub:2]]Se. Veikari sýrueiginleikar fela í sér meiri basa eiginleika."},{"key":"m68832:title:fs-idm108618080-title","en":"Structures of the Nonmetals","is":"Bygging málmleysingja"},{"key":"m68832:para:fs-idm97847936","en":"The structures of the nonmetals differ dramatically from those of metals. Metals crystallize in closely packed arrays that do not contain molecules or covalent bonds. Nonmetal structures contain covalent bonds, and many nonmetals consist of individual molecules. The electrons in nonmetals are localized in covalent bonds, whereas in a metal, there is delocalization of the electrons throughout the solid.","is":"Bygging málmleysingja er verulega frábrugðin byggingu málma. Málmar kristallast í þéttpökkuðum fylkingum sem innihalda ekki sameindir eða samgild tengi. Bygging málmleysingja inniheldur samgild tengi og margir málmleysingjar samanstanda af stökum sameindum. Rafeindirnar í málmleysingjum eru staðbundnar í samgildum tengjum, en í málmi er óstaðsetning rafeinda um allt fasta efnið."},{"key":"m68832:para:fs-idm97451120","en":"The noble gases are all monatomic, whereas the other nonmetal gases—hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine, and chlorine—normally exist as the diatomic molecules H[[sub:2,]] N[[sub:2]], O[[sub:2]], F[[sub:2]], and Cl[[sub:2]]. The other halogens are also diatomic; Br[[sub:2]] is a liquid and I[[sub:2]] exists as a solid under normal conditions. The changes in state as one moves down the halogen family offer excellent examples of the increasing strength of intermolecular London forces with increasing molecular mass and increasing polarizability.","is":"Eðallofttegundirnar eru allar einatóna, en hinar málmleysandi lofttegundirnar — vetni, köfnunarefni, súrefni, flúor og klór — eru venjulega til sem tvíatóna sameindir H[[sub:2,]] N[[sub:2]], O[[sub:2]], F[[sub:2]] og Cl[[sub:2]]. Hinir halógenarnir eru einnig tvíatóna; Br[[sub:2]] er vökvi og I[[sub:2]] er til sem fast efni við venjulegar aðstæður. Breytingar á ham þegar farið er niður halógenafjölskylduna eru frábær dæmi um aukinn styrk London-krafta milli sameinda með aukinni sameindamassa og aukinni skautanleika."},{"key":"m68832:para:fs-idm108747680","en":"Oxygen has two allotropes: O[[sub:2]], dioxygen, and O[[sub:3]], ozone. Phosphorus has three common allotropes, commonly referred to by their colors: white, red, and black. Sulfur has several allotropes. There are also many carbon allotropes. Most people know of diamond, graphite, and charcoal, but fewer people know of the recent discovery of fullerenes, carbon nanotubes, and graphene.","is":"Súrefni hefur tvær fjölmyndir: O[[sub:2]], tvísúrefni, og O[[sub:3]], óson. Fosfór hefur þrjár algengar fjölmyndir, sem venjulega er vísað til með litum þeirra: hvítur, rauður og svartur. Brennisteinn hefur nokkrar fjölmyndir. Einnig eru til margar kolefnisfjölmyndir. Flestir þekkja demant, grafít og viðarkol, en færri vita af nýlegri uppgötvun fullerenes, kolefnisnanóröra og grafens."},{"key":"m68832:para:fs-idm106007328","en":"Descriptions of the physical properties of three nonmetals that are characteristic of molecular solids follow.","is":"Lýsingar á eðliseiginleikum þriggja málmleysingja sem eru einkennandi fyrir sameindaföst efni fylgja hér á eftir."},{"key":"m68832:title:fs-idm57470288-title","en":"Carbon","is":"Kolefni"},{"key":"m68832:para:fs-idm74407552","en":"Carbon occurs in the uncombined (elemental) state in many forms, such as diamond, graphite, charcoal, coke, carbon black, graphene, and fullerene.","is":"Kolefni kemur fyrir í óbundnu (frumefnis) ástandi í mörgum myndum, svo sem demantur, grafít, viðarkol, kók, kolsót, grafen og fulleren."},{"key":"m68832:para:fs-idm64573232","en":"Diamond, shown in [[xref:CNX_Chem_18_04_Carbonform]], is a very hard crystalline material that is colorless and transparent when pure. Each atom forms four single bonds to four other atoms at the corners of a tetrahedron ([[i:sp]][[sup:3]] hybridization); this makes the diamond a giant molecule. Carbon-carbon single bonds are very strong, and, because they extend throughout the crystal to form a three-dimensional network, the crystals are very hard and have high melting points (~4400 °C).","is":"Demantur, sýndur í [[xref:CNX_Chem_18_04_Carbonform]], er mjög hart kristallað efni sem er litlaust og gegnsætt þegar það er hreint. Hvert atóm myndar fjögur eintengi við fjögur önnur atóm á hornum ferflötungs ([[i:sp]][[sup:3]] svigrúmablöndun); þetta gerir demantinn að risasameind. Kolefnis-kolefnis eintengi eru mjög sterk, og þar sem þau teygja sig um allan kristallinn til að mynda þrívítt net, eru kristallarnir mjög harðir og hafa hátt bræðslumark (~4400 °C)."},{"key":"m68832:caption:CNX_Chem_18_04_Carbonform-caption","en":"(a) Diamond and (b) graphite are two forms of carbon. (c) In the crystal structure of diamond, the covalent bonds form three-dimensional tetrahedrons. (d) In the crystal structure of graphite, each planar layer is composed of six-membered rings. (credit a: modification of work by “Fancy Diamonds”/Flickr; credit b: modification of work from http://images-of-elements.com/carbon.php)","is":"(a) Demantur og (b) grafít eru tvö form kolefnis. (c) Í kristalbyggingu demants mynda samgildu tengin þrívíða ferflötunga. (d) Í kristalbyggingu grafíts er hvert flatt lag samsett úr sexliða hringjum. (heimild a: breyting á verki eftir „Fancy Diamonds“/Flickr; heimild b: breyting á verki frá http://images-of-elements.com/carbon.php)"},{"key":"m68832:alt:fs-idm142208784-alt","en":"Two photos and two images are shown and labeled, “a,” “b,” “c,” and “d.” Photo a is of a diamond held by tweezers. Photo b shows a black columnar solid. Image c shows layered sheets of interconnected hexagonal rings. Image d shows sheets of hexagonal rings.","is":"Tvær myndir og tvær skýringarmyndir eru sýndar og merktar „a“, „b“, „c“ og „d“. Mynd a er af demanti sem haldið er með töng. Mynd b sýnir svart súlulaga fast efni. Skýringarmynd c sýnir lög af samtengdum sexhyrndum hringjum. Skýringarmynd d sýnir lög af sexhyrndum hringjum."},{"key":"m68832:para:fs-idm157413808","en":"Graphite, also shown in [[xref:CNX_Chem_18_04_Carbonform]], is a soft, slippery, grayish-black solid that conducts electricity. These properties relate to its structure, which consists of layers of carbon atoms, with each atom surrounded by three other carbon atoms in a trigonal planar arrangement. Each carbon atom in graphite forms three σ bonds, one to each of its nearest neighbors, by means of [[i:sp]][[sup:2]]-hybrid orbitals. The unhybridized [[i:p]] orbital on each carbon atom will overlap unhybridized orbitals on adjacent carbon atoms in the same layer to form π bonds. Many resonance forms are necessary to describe the electronic structure of a graphite layer; [[xref:CNX_Chem_18_04_unhyporbC]] illustrates two of these forms.","is":"Grafít, sem einnig er sýnt í [[xref:CNX_Chem_18_04_Carbonform]], er mjúkt, sleipt, grásvart fast efni sem leiðir rafmagn. Þessir eiginleikar tengjast byggingu þess, sem samanstendur af lögum af kolefnisatómum, þar sem hvert atóm er umkringt þremur öðrum kolefnisatómum í þríhyrndri flatri uppröðun. Hvert kolefnisatóm í grafíti myndar þrjú σ-tengi, eitt við hvern nálægan nágranna, með [[i:sp]][[sup:2]]-svigrúmablönduðum svigrúmum. Ósvigrúmablandað [[i:p]]-svigrúm á hverju kolefnisatómi mun skarast við ósvigrúmablönduð svigrúm á aðliggjandi kolefnisatómum í sama lagi til að mynda π-tengi. Mörg samgild form eru nauðsynleg til að lýsa rafeindabyggingu grafítlags; [[xref:CNX_Chem_18_04_unhyporbC]] sýnir tvö þessara forma."},{"key":"m68832:caption:CNX_Chem_18_04_unhyporbC-caption","en":"(a) Carbon atoms in graphite have unhybridized [[i:p]] orbitals. Each [[i:p]] orbital is perpendicular to the plane of carbon atoms. (b) These are two of the many resonance forms of graphite necessary to describe its electronic structure as a resonance hybrid.","is":"(a) Kolefnisatóm í grafíti hafa ósvigrúmablönduð [[i:p]]-svigrúm. Hvert [[i:p]]-svigrúm er hornrétt á plan kolefnisatómanna. (b) Þetta eru tvö af mörgum samgildum formum grafíts sem eru nauðsynleg til að lýsa rafeindabyggingu þess sem samgildan blending."},{"key":"m68832:alt:fs-idm54505824-alt","en":"Two images are shown and labeled, “a” and “b.” Image a shows two connected hexagonal rings, with figure-eight-shaped orbitals located at each point of the ring and in a perpendicular position. Image b shows a pair of diagrams, each of which has a series of connected hexagonal rings made up of carbon atoms that are connected by alternating single and double bonds. These two diagrams are connected by a double-headed arrow.","is":"Tvær myndir eru sýndar og merktar „a“ og „b“. Mynd a sýnir tvo samtengda sexhyrnda hringi, með átta-laga svigrúmum staðsettum á hverjum punkti hringsins og í hornréttri stöðu. Mynd b sýnir par af skýringarmyndum, sem hvor um sig hefur röð samtengdra sexhyrndra hringja úr kolefnisatómum sem eru tengd með víxlum milli eintengja og tvítengja. Þessar tvær skýringarmyndir eru tengdar með tvíhöfða ör."},{"key":"m68832:para:fs-idp56198176","en":"Atoms within a graphite layer are bonded together tightly by the σ and π bonds; however, the forces between layers are weak. London dispersion forces hold the layers together. To learn more, see the discussion of these weak forces in the chapter on liquids and solids. The weak forces between layers give graphite the soft, flaky character that makes it useful as the so-called “lead” in pencils and the slippery character that makes it useful as a lubricant. The loosely held electrons in the resonating π bonds can move throughout the solid and are responsible for the electrical conductivity of graphite.","is":"Atóm innan grafítlags eru þétt tengd saman með σ- og π-tengjum; hins vegar eru kraftarnir milli laganna veikir. London-dreifikraftar halda lögunum saman. Til að læra meira, sjá umfjöllun um þessa veiku krafta í kaflanum um vökva og föst efni. Veiku kraftarnir milli laganna gefa grafíti mjúka, flagnandi eiginleika sem gera það gagnlegt sem hið svokallaða „blý“ í blýöntum og sleipa eiginleika sem gera það gagnlegt sem smurefni. Laust haldnar rafeindir í samgildu π-tengjunum geta hreyfst um allt fasta efnið og eru ábyrgar fyrir rafleiðni grafíts."},{"key":"m68832:para:fs-idm106154768","en":"Other forms of elemental carbon include carbon black, charcoal, and coke. Carbon black is an amorphous form of carbon prepared by the incomplete combustion of natural gas, CH[[sub:4]]. It is possible to produce charcoal and coke by heating wood and coal, respectively, at high temperatures in the absence of air.","is":"Önnur form frumefnisins kolefnis eru meðal annars kolsót, viðarkol og koks. Kolsót er myndlaust form kolefnis sem er útbúið með ófullkomnum bruna á jarðgasi, CH[[sub:4]]. Hægt er að framleiða viðarkol og koks með því að hita við og kol, hvort í sínu lagi, við háan hita án lofts."},{"key":"m68832:para:fs-idm135394992","en":"Recently, new forms of elemental carbon molecules have been identified in the soot generated by a smoky flame and in the vapor produced when graphite is heated to very high temperatures in a vacuum or in helium. One of these new forms, first isolated by Professor Richard [[term:Smalley|term-00003]] and coworkers at Rice University, consists of icosahedral (soccer-ball-shaped) molecules that contain 60 carbon atoms, C[[sub:60]]. This is buckminsterfullerene (often called bucky balls) after the architect Buckminster [[term:Fuller|term-00004]], who designed domed structures, which have a similar appearance ([[xref:CNX_Chem_18_04_Buckyball]]).","is":"Nýlega hafa ný form af frumefniskolefnissameindum verið auðkennd í sóti sem myndast við reykjarmikinn loga og í gufunni sem myndast þegar grafít er hitað að mjög háum hita í lofttæmi eða í helíum. Eitt þessara nýju forma, sem fyrst var einangrað af prófessor Richard [[term:Smalley|term-00003]] og samstarfsmönnum við Rice-háskóla, samanstendur af tvítugflötungum (fótboltalaga) sameindum sem innihalda 60 kolefnisatóm, C[[sub:60]]. Þetta er buckminsterfulleren (oft kallaðar bucky-kúlur) eftir arkitektinum Buckminster [[term:Fuller|term-00004]], sem hannaði hvelfingarlaga mannvirki sem hafa svipað útlit ([[xref:CNX_Chem_18_04_Buckyball]])."},{"key":"m68832:caption:CNX_Chem_18_04_Buckyball-caption","en":"The molecular structure of C[[sub:60]], buckminsterfullerene, is icosahedral.","is":"Sameindabygging C[[sub:60]], buckminsterfullerens, er tvítugflötungur."},{"key":"m68832:alt:fs-idm51418352-alt","en":"A spherical structure is made up of hexagonal rings, each of which is made up of atoms bonded together with alternating single and double bonds.","is":"Kúlulaga bygging er gerð úr sexhyrndum hringjum, sem hver um sig er gerður úr atómum sem eru tengd saman með víxlum milli eintengja og tvítengja."},{"key":"m68832:note-title:fs-idm138324592-title","en":"Nanotubes and Graphene","is":"Nanórör og grafen"},{"key":"m68832:para:fs-idm41398960","en":"Graphene and carbon nanotubes are two recently discovered allotropes of carbon. Both of the forms bear some relationship to graphite. Graphene is a single layer of graphite (one atom thick), as illustrated in [[xref:CNX_Chem_18_04_Nanotube]], whereas carbon nanotubes roll the layer into a small tube, as illustrated in [[xref:CNX_Chem_18_04_Nanotube]].","is":"Grafen og kolefnisnanórör eru tvö nýlega uppgötvuð fjölgervingsform kolefnis. Bæði formin eiga nokkuð skylt við grafít. Grafen er eitt lag af grafíti (eins atóms þykkt), eins og sýnt er í [[xref:CNX_Chem_18_04_Nanotube]], en kolefnisnanórör rúlla laginu upp í lítið rör, eins og sýnt er í [[xref:CNX_Chem_18_04_Nanotube]]."},{"key":"m68832:para:fs-idm143379488","en":"Graphene is a very strong, lightweight, and efficient conductor of heat and electricity discovered in 2003. As in graphite, the carbon atoms form a layer of six-membered rings with [[i:sp]][[sup:2]]-hybridized carbon atoms at the corners. Resonance stabilizes the system and leads to its conductivity. Unlike graphite, there is no stacking of the layers to give a three-dimensional structure. Andre [[term:Geim|term-00005]] and Kostya [[term:Novoselov|term-00006]] at the University of Manchester won the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics for their pioneering work characterizing graphene.","is":"Grafen er mjög sterkt, létt og skilvirkur hita- og rafleiðari sem var uppgötvað árið 2003. Eins og í grafíti mynda kolefnisatómin lag af sexliða hringjum með [[i:sp]][[sup:2]]-svigrúmablönduðum kolefnisatómum á hornunum. Samgildi stöðgar kerfið og leiðir til leiðni þess. Ólíkt grafíti er engin stöflun á lögunum til að mynda þrívíða byggingu. Andre [[term:Geim|term-00005]] og Kostya [[term:Novoselov|term-00006]] við Manchester-háskóla unnu Nóbelsverðlaunin í eðlisfræði árið 2010 fyrir brautryðjendastarf sitt við að lýsa eiginleikum grafens."},{"key":"m68832:para:fs-idm162489136","en":"The simplest procedure for preparing graphene is to use a piece of adhesive tape to remove a single layer of graphene from the surface of a piece of graphite. This method works because there are only weak London dispersion forces between the layers in graphite. Alternative methods are to deposit a single layer of carbon atoms on the surface of some other material (ruthenium, iridium, or copper) or to synthesize it at the surface of silicon carbide via the sublimation of silicon.","is":"Einfaldasta aðferðin til að útbúa grafen er að nota límband til að fjarlægja eitt lag af grafeni af yfirborði grafítbúts. Þessi aðferð virkar vegna þess að það eru aðeins veikir London-dreifikraftar milli laganna í grafíti. Aðrar aðferðir eru að setja eitt lag af kolefnisatómum á yfirborð einhvers annars efnis (rúþen, iridín eða kopar) eða að mynda það á yfirborði kísilkarbíðs með þurrgufun kísils."},{"key":"m68832:para:fs-idm221903792","en":"There currently are no commercial applications of graphene. However, its unusual properties, such as high electron mobility and thermal conductivity, should make it suitable for the manufacture of many advanced electronic devices and for thermal management applications.","is":"Eins og er eru engin viðskiptaleg not fyrir grafen. Hins vegar ættu óvenjulegir eiginleikar þess, svo sem mikill rafeindahreyfanleiki og hitaleiðni, að gera það hentugt til framleiðslu á mörgum háþróuðum rafeindatækjum og fyrir hitastjórnunarlausnir."},{"key":"m68832:para:fs-idm231566608","en":"Carbon nanotubes are carbon allotropes, which have a cylindrical structure. Like graphite and graphene, nanotubes consist of rings of [[i:sp]][[sup:2]]-hybridized carbon atoms. Unlike graphite and graphene, which occur in layers, the layers wrap into a tube and bond together to produce a stable structure. The walls of the tube may be one atom or multiple atoms thick.","is":"Kolefnisnanórör eru fjölgervingsform kolefnis sem hafa sívalningslaga byggingu. Eins og grafít og grafen samanstanda nanórör af hringjum af [[i:sp]][[sup:2]]-svigrúmablönduðum kolefnisatómum. Ólíkt grafíti og grafeni, sem koma fyrir í lögum, vefjast lögin saman í rör og tengjast saman til að mynda stöðuga byggingu. Veggir rörsins geta verið eins atóms eða margra atóma þykkir."},{"key":"m68832:para:fs-idm217457872","en":"Carbon nanotubes are extremely strong materials that are harder than diamond. Depending upon the shape of the nanotube, it may be a conductor or semiconductor. For some applications, the conducting form is preferable, whereas other applications utilize the semiconducting form.","is":"Kolefnisnanórör eru afar sterk efni sem eru harðari en demantur. Það fer eftir lögun nanórörsins hvort það er leiðari eða hálfleiðari. Fyrir sum not er leiðandi formið æskilegra, en önnur not nýta hálfleiðandi formið."},{"key":"m68832:para:fs-idm97062944","en":"The basis for the synthesis of carbon nanotubes is the generation of carbon atoms in a vacuum. It is possible to produce carbon atoms by an electrical discharge through graphite, vaporization of graphite with a laser, and the decomposition of a carbon compound.","is":"Grundvöllur myndunar kolefnisnanóröra er myndun kolefnisatóma í lofttæmi. Hægt er að framleiða kolefnisatóm með rafhleðslu í gegnum grafít, gufun grafíts með leysi og niðurbroti á kolefnissambandi."},{"key":"m68832:para:fs-idp36666976","en":"The strength of carbon nanotubes will eventually lead to some of their most exciting applications, as a thread produced from several nanotubes will support enormous weight. However, the current applications only employ bulk nanotubes. The addition of nanotubes to polymers improves the mechanical, thermal, and electrical properties of the bulk material. There are currently nanotubes in some bicycle parts, skis, baseball bats, fishing rods, and surfboards.","is":"Styrkur kolefnisnanóröra mun á endanum leiða til nokkurra af mest spennandi notum þeirra, þar sem þráður framleiddur úr nokkrum nanórörum mun geta borið gríðarlega þyngd. Hins vegar eru núverandi not aðeins fyrir nanórör í lausu formi. Viðbót nanóröra við fjölliður bætir vélræna, varmafræðilega og rafmagnsfræðilega eiginleika efnisins í heild. Nú þegar eru nanórör í sumum hjólahlutum, skíðum, hafnaboltakylfum, veiðistöngum og brimbrettum."},{"key":"m68832:caption:CNX_Chem_18_04_Nanotube-caption","en":"(a) Graphene and (b) carbon nanotubes are both allotropes of carbon.","is":"(a) Grafen og (b) kolefnisnanórör eru bæði fjölgervisform kolefnis."},{"key":"m68832:alt:fs-idp35290448-alt","en":"Two images are shown and labeled “a” and “b.” Image a shows a long sheet of interconnected hexagonal rings. Image b shows the same interconnected hexagonal rings forming a curled sheet to make a long tube.","is":"Tvær myndir eru sýndar og merktar „a“ og „b“. Mynd a sýnir langa örk af samtengdum sexhyrndum hringjum. Mynd b sýnir sömu samtengdu sexhyrndu hringina mynda upprúllaða örk til að búa til langt rör."},{"key":"m68832:title:fs-idm157346064-title","en":"Phosphorus","is":"Fosfór"},{"key":"m68832:para:fs-idm188499280","en":"The name [[i:phosphorus]] comes from the Greek words meaning [[i:light bringing.]] When phosphorus was first isolated, scientists noted that it glowed in the dark and burned when exposed to air. Phosphorus is the only member of its group that does not occur in the uncombined state in nature; it exists in many allotropic forms. We will consider two of those forms: white phosphorus and red phosphorus.","is":"Nafnið [[i:fosfór]] kemur úr grísku orðunum sem þýða [[i:ljósberi]]. Þegar fosfór var fyrst einangraður tóku vísindamenn eftir því að hann ljómaði í myrkri og brann þegar hann komst í snertingu við loft. Fosfór er eini meðlimur síns flokks sem finnst ekki í óbundnu ástandi í náttúrunni; hann er til í mörgum fjölgervisformum. Við munum skoða tvö þessara forma: hvítan fosfór og rauðan fosfór."},{"key":"m68832:para:fs-idm197336480","en":"White phosphorus is a white, waxy solid that melts at 44.2 °C and boils at 280 °C. It is insoluble in water (in which it is stored—see [[xref:CNX_Chem_18_04_Phosphorus]]), is very soluble in carbon disulfide, and bursts into flame in air. As a solid, as a liquid, as a gas, and in solution, white phosphorus exists as P[[sub:4]] molecules with four phosphorus atoms at the corners of a regular tetrahedron, as illustrated in [[xref:CNX_Chem_18_04_Phosphorus]]. Each phosphorus atom covalently bonds to the other three atoms in the molecule by single covalent bonds. White phosphorus is the most reactive allotrope and is very toxic.","is":"Hvítur fosfór er hvítt, vaxkennt fast efni sem bráðnar við 44,2 °C og sýður við 280 °C. Hann er óleysanlegur í vatni (þar sem hann er geymdur – sjá [[xref:CNX_Chem_18_04_Phosphorus]]), er mjög leysanlegur í koldísúlfíði og blossar upp í lofti. Sem fast efni, sem vökvi, sem gas og í lausn er hvítur fosfór til sem P[[sub:4]] sameindir með fjórum fosfóratómum á hornum reglulegs ferflötungs, eins og sýnt er á [[xref:CNX_Chem_18_04_Phosphorus]]. Hvert fosfóratóm tengist hinum þremur atómum í sameindinni með samgildum eintengjum. Hvítur fosfór er hvarfgjarnasta fjölgervisformið og er mjög eitraður."},{"key":"m68832:caption:CNX_Chem_18_04_Phosphorus-caption","en":"(a) Because white phosphorus bursts into flame in air, it is stored in water. (b) The structure of white phosphorus consists of P[[sub:4]] molecules arranged in a tetrahedron. (c) Red phosphorus is much less reactive than is white phosphorus. (d) The structure of red phosphorus consists of networks of P[[sub:4]] tetrahedra joined by P-P single bonds. (credit a: modification of work from http://images-of-elements.com/phosphorus.php)","is":"(a) Þar sem hvítur fosfór blossar upp í lofti er hann geymdur í vatni. (b) Bygging hvíts fosfórs samanstendur af P[[sub:4]] sameindum sem raðast í ferflötung. (c) Rauður fosfór er mun minna hvarfgjarn en hvítur fosfór. (d) Bygging rauðs fosfórs samanstendur af netum P[[sub:4]] ferflötunga sem tengdir eru saman með P-P eintengjum. (heimild a: breyting á verki frá http://images-of-elements.com/phosphorus.php)"},{"key":"m68832:alt:fs-idm121503472-alt","en":"Two photos and two diagrams are shown and labeled “a,” “b,” “c,” and “d.” Photo a shows a test tube that contains a solid yellow compound. Diagram d shows two four-sided pyramid shapes that have an atom at each corner and are connected together by a single bond.","is":"Tvær ljósmyndir og tvær skýringarmyndir eru sýndar og merktar „a“, „b“, „c“ og „d“. Ljósmynd a sýnir [[test tube:tilraunaglas]] sem inniheldur fast gult efnasamband. Skýringarmynd b sýnir fjórhliða pýramídalaga form sem hefur atóm á hverju horni. Ljósmynd c sýnir dökkt svart duft í úrglasi. Skýringarmynd d sýnir tvö fjórhliða pýramídalaga form sem hafa atóm á hverju horni og eru tengd saman með eintengi."},{"key":"m68832:para:fs-idp28980160","en":"Heating white phosphorus to 270–300 °C in the absence of air yields red phosphorus. Red phosphorus (shown in [[xref:CNX_Chem_18_04_Phosphorus]]) is denser, has a higher melting point (~600 °C), is much less reactive, is essentially nontoxic, and is easier and safer to handle than is white phosphorus. Its structure is highly polymeric and appears to contain three-dimensional networks of P[[sub:4]] tetrahedra joined by P-P single bonds. Red phosphorus is insoluble in solvents that dissolve white phosphorus. When red phosphorus is heated, P[[sub:4]] molecules sublime from the solid.","is":"Með því að hita hvítan fosfór í 270–300 °C án lofts fæst rauður fosfór. Rauður fosfór (sýndur á [[xref:CNX_Chem_18_04_Phosphorus]]) er eðlisþyngri, hefur hærra bræðslumark (~600 °C), er mun minna hvarfgjarn, er í raun óeitraður og er auðveldari og öruggari í meðhöndlun en hvítur fosfór. Bygging hans er mjög fjölliðukennd og virðist innihalda þrívíð net af P[[sub:4]] ferflötungum sem tengdir eru saman með P-P eintengjum. Rauður fosfór er óleysanlegur í leysum sem leysa upp hvítan fosfór. Þegar rauður fosfór er hitaður þurrgufa P[[sub:4]] sameindir úr fasta efninu."},{"key":"m68832:title:fs-idm209718960-title","en":"Sulfur","is":"Brennisteinn"},{"key":"m68832:para:fs-idm76786544","en":"The allotropy of sulfur is far greater and more complex than that of any other element. Sulfur is the brimstone referred to in the Bible and other places, and references to sulfur occur throughout recorded history—right up to the relatively recent discovery that it is a component of the atmospheres of Venus and of Io, a moon of Jupiter. The most common and most stable allotrope of sulfur is yellow, rhombic sulfur, so named because of the shape of its crystals. Rhombic sulfur is the form to which all other allotropes revert at room temperature. Crystals of rhombic sulfur melt at 113 °C. Cooling this liquid gives long needles of monoclinic sulfur. This form is stable from 96 °C to the melting point, 119 °C. At room temperature, it gradually reverts to the rhombic form.","is":"Fjölgervisform brennisteins eru mun fleiri og flóknari en nokkurs annars frumefnis. Brennisteinn er sá eldbrennisteinn sem vísað er til í Biblíunni og víðar og tilvísanir í brennistein koma fyrir í gegnum skráða sögu – allt fram að tiltölulega nýlegri uppgötvun að hann sé hluti af lofthjúpum Venusar og Íó, tungls Júpíters. Algengasta og stöðugasta fjölgervisform brennisteins er gulur, tígullaga brennisteinn, nefndur svo vegna lögunar kristalla hans. Tígullaga brennisteinn er formið sem öll önnur fjölgervisform hverfa aftur í við stofuhita. Kristallar tígullaga brennisteins bráðna við 113 °C. Með því að kæla þennan vökva fást langar nálar af einklínum brennisteini. Þetta form er stöðugt frá 96 °C að bræðslumarki, 119 °C. Við stofuhita hverfur það smám saman aftur í tígullaga formið."},{"key":"m68832:para:fs-idm187719200","en":"Both rhombic sulfur and monoclinic sulfur contain S[[sub:8]] molecules in which atoms form eight-membered, puckered rings that resemble crowns, as illustrated in [[xref:CNX_Chem_18_04_Sulfrchain]]. Each sulfur atom is bonded to each of its two neighbors in the ring by covalent S-S single bonds.","is":"Bæði tígullaga brennisteinn og einklínn brennisteinn innihalda S[[sub:8]] sameindir þar sem atóm mynda áttaliða, bylgjótta hringi sem líkjast kórónum, eins og sýnt er á [[xref:CNX_Chem_18_04_Sulfrchain]]. Hvert brennisteinsatóm er tengt hvorum tveggja nágranna sinna í hringnum með samgildum S-S eintengjum."},{"key":"m68832:caption:CNX_Chem_18_04_Sulfrchain-caption","en":"These four sulfur allotropes show eight-membered, puckered rings. Each sulfur atom bonds to each of its two neighbors in the ring by covalent S-S single bonds. Here are (a) individual S[[sub:8]] rings, (b) S[[sub:8]] chains formed when the rings open, (c) longer chains formed by adding sulfur atoms to S[[sub:8]] chains, and (d) part of the very long sulfur chains formed at higher temperatures.","is":"Þessi fjögur fjölgervisform brennisteins sýna áttaliða, bylgjótta hringi. Hvert brennisteinsatóm tengist hvorum tveggja nágranna sinna í hringnum með samgildum S-S eintengjum. Hér eru (a) stakir S[[sub:8]] hringir, (b) S[[sub:8]] keðjur sem myndast þegar hringirnir opnast, (c) lengri keðjur sem myndast með því að bæta brennisteinsatómum við S[[sub:8]] keðjur og (d) hluti af mjög löngum brennisteinskeðjum sem myndast við hærra hitastig."},{"key":"m68832:alt:fs-idp5064384-alt","en":"Four diagrams are shown and labeled “a,” “b,” “c,” and “d.” Diagram a shows four ring structures that are each made up of eight single bonded atoms. Diagram b shows four chains of eight atoms. Diagram c shows three chains of atoms, one composed by nine atoms, one by twelve atoms and one by eleven atoms. Diagram d shows the same three chains, but this time they are much closer together and slightly intertwined.","is":"Fjórar skýringarmyndir eru sýndar og merktar „a“, „b“, „c“ og „d“. Skýringarmynd a sýnir fjórar hringlaga byggingar sem hver um sig er gerð úr átta eintengdum atómum. Skýringarmynd b sýnir fjórar keðjur með átta atómum. Skýringarmynd c sýnir þrjár keðjur af atómum, ein samsett úr níu atómum, ein úr tólf atómum og ein úr ellefu atómum. Skýringarmynd d sýnir sömu þrjár keðjurnar, en í þetta sinn eru þær mun nær hvor annarri og örlítið samfléttaðar."},{"key":"m68832:para:fs-idm163997136","en":"When rhombic sulfur melts, the straw-colored liquid is quite mobile; its viscosity is low because S[[sub:8]] molecules are essentially spherical and offer relatively little resistance as they move past each other. As the temperature rises, S-S bonds in the rings break, and polymeric chains of sulfur atoms result. These chains combine end to end, forming still longer chains that tangle with one another. The liquid gradually darkens in color and becomes so viscous that finally (at about 230 °C) it does not pour easily. The dangling atoms at the ends of the chains of sulfur atoms are responsible for the dark red color because their electronic structure differs from those of sulfur atoms that have bonds to two adjacent sulfur atoms. This causes them to absorb light differently and results in a different visible color. Cooling the liquid rapidly produces a rubberlike amorphous mass, called plastic sulfur.","is":"Þegar tígullaga brennisteinn bráðnar er stráguli vökvinn nokkuð hreyfanlegur; seigja hans er lág vegna þess að S[[sub:8]] sameindir eru í raun kúlulaga og veita tiltölulega lítið viðnám þegar þær hreyfast fram hjá hver annarri. Þegar hitastigið hækkar rofna S-S tengi í hringjunum og fjölliðukeðjur brennisteinsatóma myndast. Þessar keðjur sameinast enda við enda og mynda enn lengri keðjur sem flækjast saman. Vökvinn dökknar smám saman og verður svo seigur að loks (við um 230 °C) hellist hann ekki auðveldlega. Lausu atómin á endum brennisteinsatómakeðjanna eru ábyrg fyrir dökkrauða litnum vegna þess að rafeindabygging þeirra er frábrugðin rafeindabyggingu brennisteinsatóma sem hafa tengi við tvö aðliggjandi brennisteinsatóm. Þetta veldur því að þau gleypa ljós á annan hátt og leiðir til annars sýnilegs litar. Með því að kæla vökvann hratt myndast gúmmíkenndur myndlaus massi, sem kallast plastefnisbrennisteinn."},{"key":"m68832:para:fs-idm133348256","en":"Sulfur boils at 445 °C and forms a vapor consisting of S[[sub:2]], S[[sub:6]], and S[[sub:8]] molecules; at about 1000 °C, the vapor density corresponds to the formula S[[sub:2]], which is a paramagnetic molecule like O[[sub:2]] with a similar electronic structure and a weak sulfur-sulfur double bond.","is":"Brennisteinn sýður við 445 °C og myndar gufu sem samanstendur af S[[sub:2]], S[[sub:6]] og S[[sub:8]] sameindum; við um 1000 °C samsvarar gufuþéttleikinn formúlunni S[[sub:2]], sem er segulmögnuð sameind eins og O[[sub:2]] með svipaða rafeindabyggingu og veikt brennisteins-brennisteins tvítengi."},{"key":"m68832:para:fs-idm1928176","en":"As seen in this discussion, an important feature of the structural behavior of the nonmetals is that the elements usually occur with eight electrons in their valence shells. If necessary, the elements form enough covalent bonds to supplement the electrons already present to possess an octet. For example, members of group 15 have five valence electrons and require only three additional electrons to fill their valence shells. These elements form three covalent bonds in their free state: triple bonds in the N[[sub:2]] molecule or single bonds to three different atoms in arsenic and phosphorus. The elements of group 16 require only two additional electrons. Oxygen forms a double bond in the O[[sub:2]] molecule, and sulfur, selenium, and tellurium form two single bonds in various rings and chains. The halogens form diatomic molecules in which each atom is involved in only one bond. This provides the electron required necessary to complete the octet on the halogen atom. The noble gases do not form covalent bonds to other noble gas atoms because they already have a filled outer shell.","is":"Eins og sést í þessari umræðu er mikilvægur eiginleiki byggingarhegðunar málmleysingja að frumefnin koma venjulega fyrir með átta rafeindir í gildisrafeindahvelum sínum. Ef nauðsyn krefur mynda frumefnin nægilega mörg samgild tengi til að bæta við þær rafeindir sem þegar eru til staðar til að hafa áttund. Til dæmis hafa meðlimir flokks 15 fimm gildisrafeindir og þurfa aðeins þrjár rafeindir til viðbótar til að fylla gildisrafeindahvelin sín. Þessi frumefni mynda þrjú samgild tengi í frjálsu ástandi sínu: þrítengi í N[[sub:2]] sameindinni eða eintengi við þrjú mismunandi atóm í arseni og fosfór. Frumefni flokks 16 þurfa aðeins tvær rafeindir til viðbótar. Súrefni myndar tvítengi í O[[sub:2]] sameindinni og brennisteinn, selen og tellúr mynda tvö eintengi í ýmsum hringjum og keðjum. Halógenarnir mynda tvíatóma sameindir þar sem hvert atóm tekur þátt í aðeins einu tengi. Þetta gefur þá rafeind sem nauðsynleg er til að ljúka áttundinni á halógenatóminu. Eðallofttegundirnar mynda ekki samgild tengi við önnur eðallofttegundaatóm vegna þess að þær hafa þegar fullskipað ytra hvel."},{"key":"m68832:title:fs-idm158014192-title","en":"Key Concepts and Summary","is":"Lykilhugtök og samantekt"},{"key":"m68832:para:fs-idm131147120","en":"Nonmetals have structures that are very different from those of the metals, primarily because they have greater electronegativity and electrons that are more tightly bound to individual atoms. Most nonmetal oxides are acid anhydrides, meaning that they react with water to form acidic solutions. Molecular structures are common for most of the nonmetals, and several have multiple allotropes with varying physical properties.","is":"Málmleysingjar hafa byggingu sem er mjög frábrugðin byggingu málma, aðallega vegna þess að þeir hafa meiri rafneikvæðni og rafeindir sem eru fastar bundnar einstökum atómum. Flest málmleysingjaoxíð eru sýruanhýdríð, sem þýðir að þau hvarfast við vatn og mynda súrar lausnir. Sameindabyggingar eru algengar fyrir flesta málmleysingja og nokkrir hafa margar fjölmyndir með mismunandi eðliseiginleika."},{"key":"m68832:title:fs-idm161057120-title","en":"Chemistry End of Chapter Exercises","is":"Efnafræði - Lokaæfingar kafla"},{"key":"m68832:problem:fs-idm198906624","en":"Carbon forms a number of allotropes, two of which are graphite and diamond. Silicon has a diamond structure. Why is there no allotrope of silicon with a graphite structure?","is":"Kolefni myndar nokkrar fjölmyndir, þar af tvær grafít og demantur. Kísill hefur demantsbyggingu. # Editing an Icelandic machine translation of a chemistry textbook (fable-editor, version 1)

You are editing the Icelandic machine translation of an English chemistry textbook (OpenStax _Chemistry 2e_),
which is being published as a free textbook for Icelandic upper-secondary students (aged about 16 to 20).
Work as an experienced Icelandic editor (yfirlesari) with a good knowledge of chemistry.

The goal is text a student can learn from: correct Icelandic in a register that is semi-academic but fluent
for younger readers. Judge grammar, agreement, word order and word choice in context, sentence by sentence and
across the passage. The translation must stay faithful to the English: do not add, drop or localize content
(units, examples and names stay as in the English), and do not explain more than the English does.

## What you receive

One JSON document (`"format": "fable-editor-user/1"`):

- `chapter` and `module`: where the text comes from.
- `englishContext`: the whole module in English, for context. Read it to understand the passage; edit only
  the `segments`.
- `terms`: the project's house terminology for this text. Each entry has the English forms (`en`) and the
  ruled Icelandic (`is`); `avoid` lists renderings known to be wrong for it. Use the ruled term, inflected as
  the sentence needs, wherever the English uses that term in that sense. Where no ruled term applies, choose
  the established Icelandic chemistry term.
- `segments`: in document order, each with a `key`, the English (`en`) and the machine translation (`is`).
  Segments are sentences, paragraphs, captions, list items, table cells or titles.

Both texts hold inline markers in double square brackets, such as `[[term:millikrafta|term-00001]]`,
`[[i:aq]]`, `[[sub:2]]`, `[[MATH:3]]`, `[[xref:CNX_Chem_10_01_KMTPhases1]]` or
`[[link:gagnvirku hermun|http://openstax.org/l/16phetvisual]]`. They carry formatting, formulas and
references. Keep every marker, with the same type and the same number of markers in the segment. You may edit
the Icelandic words inside a `term`, `link`, `i`, `b`, `em` or `u` marker, but never the part after `|`, and
never the contents of `MATH`, `MEDIA`, `TABLE`, `xref` or `docref` markers, or of `sub` and `sup` markers that
hold formula parts. You may move a marker within the segment when Icelandic word order needs it.

## What to return

Only the segments you change, each with its `key`, the whole edited Icelandic text of that segment, and one or
more tags saying what kind of change you made:

- `terminology`: a term changed to the house term or the established term;
- `grammar`: inflection, agreement, case, or another grammatical error;
- `fluency`: word order, phrasing or idiom, so the sentence reads as natural Icelandic;
- `meaning`: the translation said something the English does not;
- `register`: too formal, too colloquial, or too hard for the readers;
- `punctuation`: punctuation, capitals, spacing or number format.

Leave a segment out when it is already good. Each key appears at most once. Change only what improves the
text; a good machine-translated sentence does not need rewording.

{"format":"fable-editor-user/1","chapter":"ch18","module":"m68833","englishContext":"Occurrence, Preparation, and Compounds of Hydrogen

By the end of this section, you will be able to:

Describe the properties, preparation, and compounds of hydrogen

Hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe. The sun and other stars are composed largely of hydrogen. Astronomers estimate that 90% of the atoms in the universe are hydrogen atoms. Hydrogen is a component of more compounds than any other element. Water is the most abundant compound of hydrogen found on earth. Hydrogen is an important part of petroleum, many minerals, cellulose and starch, sugar, fats, oils, alcohols, acids, and thousands of other substances.

At ordinary temperatures, hydrogen is a colorless, odorless, tasteless, and nonpoisonous gas consisting of the diatomic molecule H[[sub:2]]. Hydrogen is composed of three isotopes, and unlike other elements, these isotopes have different names and chemical symbols: protium, [[sup:1]]H, deuterium, [[sup:2]]H (or “D”), and tritium [[sup:3]]H (or “T”). In a naturally occurring sample of hydrogen, there is one atom of deuterium for every 7000 H atoms and one atom of radioactive tritium for every 10[[sup:18]] H atoms. The chemical properties of the different isotopes are very similar because they have identical electron structures, but they differ in some physical properties because of their differing atomic masses. Elemental deuterium and tritium have lower vapor pressure than ordinary hydrogen. Consequently, when liquid hydrogen evaporates, the heavier isotopes are concentrated in the last portions to evaporate. Electrolysis of heavy water, D[[sub:2]]O, yields deuterium. Most tritium originates from nuclear reactions.

Preparation of Hydrogen

From Steam and Carbon or Hydrocarbons

Water is the cheapest and most abundant source of hydrogen. Passing steam over coke (an impure form of elemental carbon) at 1000 °C produces a mixture of carbon monoxide and hydrogen known as water gas:

Water gas is as an industrial fuel. It is possible to produce additional hydrogen by mixing the water gas with steam in the presence of a catalyst to convert the CO to CO[[sub:2]]. This reaction is the water gas shift reaction.

It is also possible to prepare a mixture of hydrogen and carbon monoxide by passing hydrocarbons from natural gas or petroleum and steam over a nickel-based catalyst. Propane is an example of a hydrocarbon reactant:

Electrolysis

Hydrogen forms when direct current electricity passes through water containing an electrolyte such as H[[sub:2]]SO[[sub:4]], as illustrated in [[xref:CNX_Chem_18_05_Electrolys]]. Bubbles of hydrogen form at the cathode, and oxygen evolves at the anode. The net reaction is:

The electrolysis of water produces hydrogen and oxygen. Because there are twice as many hydrogen atoms as oxygen atoms and both elements are diatomic, there is twice the volume of hydrogen produced at the cathode as there is oxygen produced at the anode.

A diagram shows a beaker that contains a liquid, a battery submerged in the liquid, and two test tubes. The battery has the positive and negative terminals labeled. The liquid is connected by a right-facing arrow to an image of two molecules made up of one red atom and two white atoms. It is labeled, “Water,” and, “2 H subscript 2 O ( l ).” The left test tube above the negative sign is connected by a right-facing arrow to an image of two pairs of white atoms. The image is labeled, “Hydrogen,” and, “2 H subscript 2 ( g ).” The right test tube above the positive sign is connected by a right-facing arrow to an image of a pair of red atoms. The image is labeled, “Oxygen,” and, “O subscript 2 ( g ).”

Reaction of Metals with Acids

This is the most convenient laboratory method of producing hydrogen. Metals with lower reduction potentials reduce the hydrogen ion in dilute acids to produce hydrogen gas and metal salts. For example, as shown in [[xref:CNX_Chem_18_05_IronHCl]], iron in dilute hydrochloric acid produces hydrogen gas and iron(II) chloride:

The reaction of iron with an acid produces hydrogen. Here, iron reacts with hydrochloric acid. (credit: Mark Ott)

A photo shows a beaker that contains a clear, colorless liquid. It is labeled, “H C l ( a q ).” Beside the beaker is a watch glass with a dropper above it. The dropper is releasing liquid into a fizzing liquid. The fizzing liquid is releasing a white gas.

Reaction of Ionic Metal Hydrides with Water

It is possible to produce hydrogen from the reaction of hydrides of the active metals, which contain the very strongly basic H[[sup:−]] anion, with water:

Metal hydrides are expensive but convenient sources of hydrogen, especially where space and weight are important factors. They are important in the inflation of life jackets, life rafts, and military balloons.

Elemental hydrogen must be prepared from compounds by breaking chemical bonds. The most common methods of preparing hydrogen follow.

Reactions

Reactions with Elements

When heated, hydrogen reacts with the metals of group 1 and with Ca, Sr, and Ba (the more active metals in group 2). The compounds formed are crystalline, ionic hydrides that contain the hydride anion, H[[sup:−]], a strong reducing agent and a strong base, which reacts vigorously with water and other acids to form hydrogen gas.

The reactions of hydrogen with nonmetals generally produce [[i:acidic]] hydrogen compounds with hydrogen in the 1+ oxidation state. The reactions become more exothermic and vigorous as the electronegativity of the nonmetal increases. Hydrogen reacts with nitrogen and sulfur only when heated, but it reacts explosively with fluorine (forming HF) and, under some conditions, with chlorine (forming HCl). A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen explodes if ignited. Because of the explosive nature of the reaction, it is necessary to exercise caution when handling hydrogen (or any other combustible gas) to avoid the formation of an explosive mixture in a confined space. Although most hydrides of the nonmetals are acidic, ammonia and phosphine (PH[[sub:3]]) are very, very weak acids and generally function as bases. There is a summary of these reactions of hydrogen with the elements in [[xref:fs-idp87200896]].

This table has two columns and seven rows. The first row is a header row and it labels each column, “General Equation” and “Comments.” Under the “General Equation” column are the following equations: M H or M H subscript 2 yields M O H or M ( O H ) subscript 2 plus H subscript 2; H subscript 2 plus C yields ( no reaction ); 2 H subscript 2 plus N subscript 2 yields 2 N H subscript 3; 2 H subscript 2 plus O subscript 2 yields 2 H subscript 2 O; H subscript 2 plus S yields H subscript 2 S; and H subscript 2 plus X subscript 2 yields 2 H X. Under the “Comments” column are the following: “ionic hydrides with group 1 and C a, S r, and B a,” nothing, “requires high pressure and temperature; low yield,” “exothermic and potentially explosive,” “requires heating; low yield,” and “X equals F, C l, B r, and I; explosive with F subscript 2; low yield with I subscript 2.”

Chemical Reactions of Hydrogen with Other Elements

General Equation

Comments

[[MATH:2]]

[[MATH:4]]

[[MATH:5]]

requires heating; low yield

[[MATH:6]]

X = F, Cl, Br, and I; explosive with F[[sub:2]]; low yield with I[[sub:2]]

Reaction with Compounds

Hydrogen reduces the heated oxides of many metals, with the formation of the metal and water vapor. For example, passing hydrogen over heated CuO forms copper and water.

Hydrogen may also reduce the metal ions in some metal oxides to lower oxidation states:

Under normal conditions, hydrogen is relatively inactive chemically, but when heated, it enters into many chemical reactions.

Two thirds of the world’s hydrogen production is devoted to the manufacture of ammonia, which is a fertilizer and used in the manufacture of nitric acid. Large quantities of hydrogen are also important in the process of [[term:hydrogenation|term-00001]], discussed in the chapter on organic chemistry.

It is possible to use hydrogen as a nonpolluting fuel. The reaction of hydrogen with oxygen is a very exothermic reaction, releasing 286 kJ of energy per mole of water formed. Hydrogen burns without explosion under controlled conditions. The oxygen-hydrogen torch, because of the high heat of combustion of hydrogen, can achieve temperatures up to 2800 °C. The hot flame of this torch is useful in cutting thick sheets of many metals. Liquid hydrogen is also an important rocket fuel ([[xref:CNX_Chem_18_05_LiqHliqO]]).

Before the fleet’s retirement in 2011, liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen were used in the three main engines of a space shuttle. Two compartments in the large tank held these liquids until the shuttle was launched. (credit: “reynermedia”/Flickr)

A rocket is shown taking off.

An uncombined hydrogen atom consists of a nucleus and one valence electron in the 1[[i:s]] orbital. The [[i:n]] = 1 valence shell has a capacity for two electrons, and hydrogen can rightfully occupy two locations in the periodic table. It is possible to consider hydrogen a group 1 element because hydrogen can lose an electron to form the cation, H[[sup:+]]. It is also possible to consider hydrogen to be a group 17 element because it needs only one electron to fill its valence orbital to form a hydride ion, H[[sup:−]], or it can share an electron to form a single, covalent bond. In reality, hydrogen is a unique element that almost deserves its own location in the periodic table.

Hydrogen Compounds

Nitrogen Hydrogen Compounds

Ammonia, NH[[sub:3]], forms naturally when any nitrogen-containing organic material decomposes in the absence of air. The laboratory preparation of ammonia is by the reaction of an ammonium salt with a strong base such as sodium hydroxide. The acid-base reaction with the weakly acidic ammonium ion gives ammonia, illustrated in [[xref:CNX_Chem_18_05_Ammonia]]. Ammonia also forms when ionic nitrides react with water. The nitride ion is a much stronger base than the hydroxide ion:

The commercial production of ammonia is by the direct combination of the elements in the [[term:Haber process|term-00002]]:

The structure of ammonia is shown with a central nitrogen atom and three hydrogen atoms.

A ball-and-stick model shows a nitrogen atom single bonded to three hydrogen atoms. There is a lone pair of electron dots that appears above the nitrogen atom.

Ammonia is a colorless gas with a sharp, pungent odor. Smelling salts utilize this powerful odor. Gaseous ammonia readily liquefies to give a colorless liquid that boils at −33 °C. Due to intermolecular hydrogen bonding, the enthalpy of vaporization of liquid ammonia is higher than that of any other liquid except water, so ammonia is useful as a refrigerant. Ammonia is quite soluble in water (658 L at STP dissolves in 1 L H[[sub:2]]O).

The chemical properties of ammonia are as follows:

Ammonia acts as a Brønsted base, as discussed in the chapter on acid-base chemistry. The ammonium ion is similar in size to the potassium ion; compounds of the two ions exhibit many similarities in their structures and solubilities.

Ammonia can display acidic behavior, although it is a much weaker acid than water. Like other acids, ammonia reacts with metals, although it is so weak that high temperatures are necessary. Hydrogen and (depending on the stoichiometry) amides (salts of [[MATH:7]] imides (salts of NH[[sup:2−]]), or nitrides (salts of N[[sup:3−]]) form.

The nitrogen atom in ammonia has its lowest possible oxidation state (3−) and thus is not susceptible to reduction. However, it can be oxidized. Ammonia burns in air, giving NO and water. Hot ammonia and the ammonium ion are active reducing agents. Of particular interest are the oxidations of ammonium ion by nitrite ion, [[MATH:8]] to yield pure nitrogen and by nitrate ion to yield nitrous oxide, N[[sub:2]]O.

There are a number of compounds that we can consider derivatives of ammonia through the replacement of one or more hydrogen atoms with some other atom or group of atoms. Inorganic derivations include chloramine, NH[[sub:2]]Cl, and hydrazine, N[[sub:2]]H[[sub:4]]:

Three Lewis structures are pictured and labeled, “a,” “b,” and “c.” Structure a shows a nitrogen atom with one lone pair of electrons single bonded to three hydrogen atoms. The structure is labeled “ammonia.” Structure b shows a nitrogen atom with one lone pair of electrons single bonded to two hydrogen atoms and a chlorine atom with three lone pairs of electrons. The structure is labeled “chloramine.” Structure c shows two nitrogen atoms, each with one lone pair of electrons, single bonded to one another and each single bonded to two hydrogen atoms. The structure is labeled “hydrazine.”

Chloramine, NH[[sub:2]]Cl, results from the reaction of sodium hypochlorite, NaOCl, with ammonia in basic solution. In the presence of a large excess of ammonia at low temperature, the chloramine reacts further to produce hydrazine, N[[sub:2]]H[[sub:4]]:

Anhydrous hydrazine is relatively stable in spite of its positive free energy of formation:

Hydrazine is a fuming, colorless liquid that has some physical properties remarkably similar to those of H[[sub:2]]O (it melts at 2 °C, boils at 113.5 °C, and has a density at 25 °C of 1.00 g/mL). It burns rapidly and completely in air with substantial evolution of heat:

Like ammonia, hydrazine is both a Brønsted base and a Lewis base, although it is weaker than ammonia. It reacts with strong acids and forms two series of salts that contain the [[MATH:9]] and [[MATH:10]] ions, respectively. Some rockets use hydrazine as a fuel.

Phosphorus Hydrogen Compounds

The most important hydride of phosphorus is phosphine, PH[[sub:3]], a gaseous analog of ammonia in terms of both formula and structure. Unlike ammonia, it is not possible to form phosphine by direct union of the elements. There are two methods for the preparation of phosphine. One method is by the action of an acid on an ionic phosphide. The other method is the disproportionation of white phosphorus with hot concentrated base to produce phosphine and the hydrogen phosphite ion:

Phosphine is a colorless, very poisonous gas, which has an odor like that of decaying fish. Heat easily decomposes phosphine [[MATH:11]] and the compound burns in air. The major uses of phosphine are as a fumigant for grains and in semiconductor processing. Like ammonia, gaseous phosphine unites with gaseous hydrogen halides, forming phosphonium compounds like PH[[sub:4]]Cl and PH[[sub:4]]I. Phosphine is a much weaker base than ammonia; therefore, these compounds decompose in water, and the insoluble PH[[sub:3]] escapes from solution.

Sulfur Hydrogen Compounds

Hydrogen sulfide, H[[sub:2]]S, is a colorless gas that is responsible for the offensive odor of rotten eggs and of many hot springs. Hydrogen sulfide is as toxic as hydrogen cyanide; therefore, it is necessary to exercise great care in handling it. Hydrogen sulfide is particularly deceptive because it paralyzes the olfactory nerves; after a short exposure, one does not smell it.

The production of hydrogen sulfide by the direct reaction of the elements (H[[sub:2]] + S) is unsatisfactory because the yield is low. A more effective preparation method is the reaction of a metal sulfide with a dilute acid. For example:

It is easy to oxidize the sulfur in metal sulfides and in hydrogen sulfide, making metal sulfides and H[[sub:2]]S good reducing agents. In acidic solutions, hydrogen sulfide reduces Fe[[sup:3+]] to Fe[[sup:2+]], [[MATH:12]] to Mn[[sup:2+]], [[MATH:13]] to Cr[[sup:3+]], and HNO[[sub:3]] to NO[[sub:2]]. The sulfur in H[[sub:2]]S usually oxidizes to elemental sulfur, unless a large excess of the oxidizing agent is present. In which case, the sulfide may oxidize to [[MATH:14]] or [[MATH:15]] (or to SO[[sub:2]] or SO[[sub:3]] in the absence of water):

This oxidation process leads to the removal of the hydrogen sulfide found in many sources of natural gas. The deposits of sulfur in volcanic regions may be the result of the oxidation of H[[sub:2]]S present in volcanic gases.

Hydrogen sulfide is a weak diprotic acid that dissolves in water to form hydrosulfuric acid. The acid ionizes in two stages, yielding hydrogen sulfide ions, HS[[sup:−]], in the first stage and sulfide ions, S[[sup:2−]], in the second. Since hydrogen sulfide is a weak acid, aqueous solutions of soluble sulfides and hydrogen sulfides are basic:

Halogen Hydrogen Compounds

Binary compounds containing only hydrogen and a halogen are [[term:hydrogen halides|term-00003]]. At room temperature, the pure hydrogen halides HF, HCl, HBr, and HI are gases.

In general, it is possible to prepare the halides by the general techniques used to prepare other acids. Fluorine, chlorine, and bromine react directly with hydrogen to form the respective hydrogen halide. This is a commercially important reaction for preparing hydrogen chloride and hydrogen bromide.

The acid-base reaction between a nonvolatile strong acid and a metal halide will yield a hydrogen halide. The escape of the gaseous hydrogen halide drives the reaction to completion. For example, the usual method of preparing hydrogen fluoride is by heating a mixture of calcium fluoride, CaF[[sub:2]], and concentrated sulfuric acid:

Gaseous hydrogen fluoride is also a by-product in the preparation of phosphate fertilizers by the reaction of fluoroapatite, Ca[[sub:5]](PO[[sub:4]])[[sub:3]]F, with sulfuric acid. The reaction of concentrated sulfuric acid with a chloride salt produces hydrogen chloride both commercially and in the laboratory.

In most cases, sodium chloride is the chloride of choice because it is the least expensive chloride. Hydrogen bromide and hydrogen iodide cannot be prepared using sulfuric acid because this acid is an oxidizing agent capable of oxidizing both bromide and iodide. However, it is possible to prepare both hydrogen bromide and hydrogen iodide using an acid such as phosphoric acid because it is a weaker oxidizing agent. For example:

All of the hydrogen halides are very soluble in water, forming hydrohalic acids. With the exception of hydrogen fluoride, which has a strong hydrogen-fluoride bond, they are strong acids. Reactions of hydrohalic acids with metals, metal hydroxides, oxides, or carbonates produce salts of the halides. Most chloride salts are soluble in water. AgCl, PbCl[[sub:2]], and Hg[[sub:2]]Cl[[sub:2]] are the commonly encountered exceptions.

The halide ions give the substances the properties associated with X[[sup:−]]([[i:aq]]). The heavier halide ions (Cl[[sup:−]], Br[[sup:−]], and I[[sup:−]]) can act as reducing agents, and the lighter halogens or other oxidizing agents will oxidize them:

For example, bromine oxidizes iodine:

Hydrofluoric acid is unique in its reactions with sand (silicon dioxide) and with glass, which is a mixture of silicates:

The volatile silicon tetrafluoride escapes from these reactions. Because hydrogen fluoride attacks glass, it can frost or etch glass and is used to etch markings on thermometers, burets, and other glassware.

The largest use for hydrogen fluoride is in production of hydrochlorofluorocarbons for refrigerants, in plastics, and in propellants. The second largest use is in the manufacture of cryolite, Na[[sub:3]]AlF[[sub:6]], which is important in the production of aluminum. The acid is also important in the production of other inorganic fluorides (such as BF[[sub:3]]), which serve as catalysts in the industrial synthesis of certain organic compounds.

Hydrochloric acid is relatively inexpensive. It is an important and versatile acid in industry and is important for the manufacture of metal chlorides, dyes, glue, glucose, and various other chemicals. A considerable amount is also important for the activation of oil wells and as pickle liquor—an acid used to remove oxide coating from iron or steel that is to be galvanized, tinned, or enameled. The amounts of hydrobromic acid and hydroiodic acid used commercially are insignificant by comparison.

Other than the noble gases, each of the nonmetals forms compounds with hydrogen. For brevity, we will discuss only a few hydrogen compounds of the nonmetals here.

Key Concepts and Summary

Hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe and its chemistry is truly unique. Although it has some chemical reactivity that is similar to that of the alkali metals, hydrogen has many of the same chemical properties of a nonmetal with a relatively low electronegativity. It forms ionic hydrides with active metals, covalent compounds in which it has an oxidation state of 1− with less electronegative elements, and covalent compounds in which it has an oxidation state of 1+ with more electronegative nonmetals. It reacts explosively with oxygen, fluorine, and chlorine, less readily with bromine, and much less readily with iodine, sulfur, and nitrogen. Hydrogen reduces the oxides of metals with lower reduction potentials than chromium to form the metal and water. The hydrogen halides are all acidic when dissolved in water.

Chemistry End of Chapter Exercises

Why does hydrogen not exhibit an oxidation state of 1− when bonded to nonmetals?

The electronegativity of the nonmetals is greater than that of hydrogen. Thus, the negative charge is better represented on the nonmetal, which has the greater tendency to attract electrons in the bond to itself.

The reaction of calcium hydride, CaH[[sub:2]], with water can be characterized as a Lewis acid-base reaction:[[BR]] [[MATH:16]]

Identify the Lewis acid and the Lewis base among the reactants. The reaction is also an oxidation-reduction reaction. Identify the oxidizing agent, the reducing agent, and the changes in oxidation number that occur in the reaction.

In drawing Lewis structures, we learn that a hydrogen atom forms only one bond in a covalent compound. Why?

Hydrogen has only one orbital with which to bond to other atoms. Consequently, only one two-electron bond can form.

What mass of CaH[[sub:2]] is necessary to react with water to provide enough hydrogen gas to fill a balloon at 20 °C and 0.8 atm pressure with a volume of 4.5 L? The balanced equation is:[[BR]] [[MATH:17]]

What mass of hydrogen gas results from the reaction of 8.5 g of KH with water?[[BR]] [[MATH:18]]

0.43 g H[[sub:2]]

Hydrogen is composed of three isotopes, and unlike other elements, these isotopes have different names and chemical symbols: protium, [[sup:1]]H, deuterium, [[sup:2]]H (or “D”), and tritium [[sup:3]]H (or “T”). In a naturally occurring sample of hydrogen, there is one atom of deuterium for every 7000 H atoms and one atom of radioactive tritium for every 10[[sup:18]] H atoms. The chemical properties of the different isotopes are very similar because they have identical electron structures, but they differ in some physical properties because of their differing atomic masses. Elemental deuterium and tritium have lower vapor pressure than ordinary hydrogen. Consequently, when liquid hydrogen evaporates, the heavier isotopes are concentrated in the last portions to evaporate. Electrolysis of heavy water, D[[sub:2]]O, yields deuterium. Most tritium originates from nuclear reactions.","is":"Við venjulegt hitastig er vetni litlaus, lyktarlaus, bragðlaus og óeitrað gas sem samanstendur af tvíatóma sameindinni H[[sub:2]]. Í náttúrulegu sýni af vetni er eitt atóm af tvívetni fyrir hver 7000 H-atóm og eitt atóm af geislavirku þrívetni fyrir hver 10[[sup:18]] H-atóm. Efnafræðilegir eiginleikar mismunandi samsæta eru mjög svipaðir þar sem þær hafa eins rafeindaskipan, en þær eru ólíkar að sumum eðlisfræðilegum eiginleikum vegna mismunandi atómmassa. Frumefnin tvívetni og þrívetni hafa lægri gufuþrýsting en venjulegt vetni. Hydrogen reacts with nitrogen and sulfur only when heated, but it reacts explosively with fluorine (forming HF) and, under some conditions, with chlorine (forming HCl). A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen explodes if ignited. Because of the explosive nature of the reaction, it is necessary to exercise caution when handling hydrogen (or any other combustible gas) to avoid the formation of an explosive mixture in a confined space. Although most hydrides of the nonmetals are acidic, ammonia and phosphine (PH[[sub:3]]) are very, very weak acids and generally function as bases. The [[i:n]] = 1 valence shell has a capacity for two electrons, and hydrogen can rightfully occupy two locations in the periodic table. It is possible to consider hydrogen a group 1 element because hydrogen can lose an electron to form the cation, H[[sup:+]]. It is also possible to consider hydrogen to be a group 17 element because it needs only one electron to fill its valence orbital to form a hydride ion, H[[sup:−]], or it can share an electron to form a single, covalent bond. In reality, hydrogen is a unique element that almost deserves its own location in the periodic table.","is":"Óbundið vetnisatóm samanstendur af kjarna og einni gildisrafeind á 1[[i:s]] svigrúmi.
